PART B2
Read Text 5 and answer questions 43–62 in the Question-Answer Book for Part
B2.
Text 5
Bad Science
[1] In his seminal book ‘Bad Science’, physician and science writer Ben Goldacre
uncovers some of the flaws in science and medicine that have led to widespread
misconceptions. From the techniques employed by advertisers and the media, he
shows how little veracious scientific evidence there is to be found in their
seemingly bodacious claims. Goldacre’s book, catering to the general reader,
shows us the need to be critical of what we read.
[2] Below is the introduction excerpted from the book.
[3] Let me tell you how bad things have become. Children are being routinely
taught in thousands of British schools that if they wiggle their head up and
down it will increase blood flow to the brain, thus improving concentration;
that rubbing their fingers together in a special ‘sciencey’ way will improve
energy flow through the body, and that holding water on their tongue will
hydrate the brain directly through the roof of the mouth, all as part of a special
exercise programme called Brain Gym. We will devote some time to these beliefs
and, more importantly, the fools in our education system who endorse them.

[4] But this book is not a collection of trivial absurdities. It follows a natural
development from the foolishness of ‘experts’, via the credence they are given in
the mainstream media, through the tricks of the £30 billion food supplements
industry, the evils of the £300 billion pharmaceutical industry, the tragedy of
science reporting, and on to the poor understanding of statistics and evidence
that pervades our society.
[5] Today, scientists and doctors find themselves outnumbered and outgunned
by vast armies of individuals who feel entitled to pass judgement on matters of
evidence, an admirable aspiration, without troubling themselves to obtain a
basic understanding of the issues.
[6] At school, you were taught about chemicals in test tubes, equations to
describe motion, and maybe something on photosynthesis, but in all likelihood
you were taught nothing about death, risk, statistics, and the science of what
will kill or cure you. The hole in our culture is gaping: evidence-based medicine,
the ultimate applied science, contains some of the cleverest ideas from the past
two centuries. It has saved millions of lives, but there has never once been a
single exhibit on the subject in London’s Science Museum.
[7] This is not for a lack of interest. We are obsessed with health – half of all
science stories in the media are medical – and are repeatedly bombarded with
sciencey-sounding claims and stories. But as you will see, we get our
information from the very people who have repeatedly demonstrated themselves
to be incapable of reading, interpreting and bearing reliable witness to the
scientific evidence.
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

[8] Before we get started, let me map out the territory.
[9] Firstly, we will look at what it means to do an experiment, to see the final
results with your own eyes, and judge whether they fit with a given theory, or
whether an alternative is more compelling. You may find going through these
steps childish and patronising. The examples we look at are certainly absurd but
they have all been promoted credulously and with great authority in the
mainstream media. We will look at the attraction of sciencey-sounding stories
about our bodies, and the confusion they can cause.
[10] Interestingly our next focus is homeopathy, which Wikipedia declares as a
pseudo-science that ‘works’. We will look at this not because it’s important or
dangerous – it’s not – but because it is the perfect model for teaching
evidence-based medicine and how we can be misled into thinking that any
intervention is more effective than it really is.

[11] Then we will move onto bigger fish. Some alternative therapists claim to be
nutritionists and have somehow managed to brand themselves as men and
women of science. Their errors are interesting because they have a grain of
science to them, and that makes them not only more interesting, but also more
dangerous, because the real threat is not that their customers might die (there is
the odd case) but that they systematically undermine the public’s understanding
of the very nature of evidence.
[12] We will see the rhetorical sleights of hand and amateurish errors that have
led to you being repeatedly misled about food and nutrition. This new industry
acts as a distraction from the genuine lifestyle risk factors for ill health, as well
as its more subtle and alarming impact on the way we see ourselves and our
bodies. This arises from the widespread move to medicalise social and political
problems, to conceive of them in a reductionist, biomedical framework, and
push commodifiable solutions, particularly in the form of pills and faddish
diets. I will show you evidence that a vanguard of startling wrongness is
entering British universities, alongside genuine academic research into
nutrition. In the field of medicine, we see similar tricks used by the
pharmaceutical industry to pull the wool over the eyes of doctors and patients.

[13] Next, we will examine how the media promote the public
misunderstanding of science, their single-minded passion for pointless
non-stories, and their basic misunderstanding of statistics and evidence, which
illustrate the very core of why we do science: to prevent ourselves from being
misled by our own atomised experiences and prejudices. Finally, in the part of
the book I find most worrying, we will see how people in positions of great
power, who should know better, still commit basic errors, with grave
consequences, and we will see how the media’s cynical distortion of evidence in
two specific health scares reached dangerous and frankly grotesque extremes. It’s
your job to notice, as we go, how incredibly prevalent this stuff is, but also, to
think what you might do about it.
[14] You cannot reason people out of positions they didn’t reason themselves
into. But by the end of this book you’ll have the tools to win – or at least
understand – any argument you choose to initiate, whether it’s on miracle cures,
the evils of big pharma, the likelihood of a given vegetable preventing cancer,
and more. You’ll have seen the evidence behind some very popular deceptions,
but along the way you’ll also have picked up everything useful there is to know
about research, levels of evidence, bias, statistics, the history of science and
anti-science movements, as well as falling over just some of the amazing stories
that the natural sciences can tell us about the world along the way.
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Title
Bad Science
壞科學／錯誤科學
Paragraph 1
Background
In his seminal book ‘Bad Science’, physician and science writer Ben Goldacre
uncovers some of the flaws in science and medicine that have led to widespread
misconceptions.
在他的經典著作《Bad Science》中，醫生兼科學作家 Ben Goldacre 揭示了科學與
醫學中一些造成廣泛誤解的缺陷。
Elaboration
From the techniques employed by advertisers and the media, he shows how little
veracious scientific evidence there is to be found in their seemingly bodacious
claims.
他透過分析廣告商與媒體所採用的手法，指出那些看似驚人的說法背後，其
實往往缺乏真正可靠的科學證據。
Purpose / Conclusion
Goldacre’s book, catering to the general reader, shows us the need to be critical
of what we read.
Goldacre 這本面向一般讀者的書提醒我們：我們有必要對自己讀到的內容保
持批判思考。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

整篇文章的主線可以分成六層：
第一層，
Goldacre 先用 Brain Gym 作開場。
這些說法包括搖頭會增加腦部血流、搓手指會改善能量流動、把水含在舌頭
上可以經口腔上方直接為大腦補水。
這些例子本身看似荒唐，但作者用它們展示：
披上「科學味」外衣的說法，可以進入學校，甚至由教育系統支持。
第二層，作者把問題擴大。
這本書並非只收集笑話式的荒謬案例，是要從專家愚昧、媒體信任、食品補
充劑產業、製藥業、科學報道、統計與證據理解不足等方面，
展示整個社會如何容易被錯誤科學訊息影響。
第三層，作者指出科學家和醫生處於弱勢。
他們面對大量自以為有權判斷證據、卻缺乏基本理解的人。
這一層把問題從個別錯誤提升到公共討論的失衡。
第四層，作者批評教育與文化。學校教了化學、物理、生物等傳統知識，卻很
少教死亡、風險、統計、證據醫學，以及哪些東西會殺死你或治好你。這造成
一個巨大的文化缺口。

為甚麼答案是 bigger fish?
1. “Then” 顯示 paragraph 11 是從上一段轉入新對象
Paragraph 11 一開始的 Then 很重要。
它不是一個隨意連接詞。
它表示 Goldacre 正在按順序介紹書中接下來會處理的內容：
● firstly：experiment
● next：homeopathy
● then：bigger fish
所以 bigger fish 是一個結構性標記。
它告訴讀者：作者現在要從 homeopathy 轉去更嚴重、更值得處理的對象。
下一句馬上說：
Some alternative therapists claim to be nutritionists...
因此，這些 some alternative therapists 就是剛剛所說的 bigger fish。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

● more important targets
● more serious cases
● more significant problems
● people / issues more worth dealing with

● 更大的目標
● 更嚴重的對象
● 更值得處理的一批人
● 更棘手的問題

“But by the end of this book you’ll have the tools to win – or at least
understand – any argument you choose to initiate, whether it’s on miracle
cures, the evils of big pharma, the likelihood of a given vegetable preventing
cancer, and more. You’ll have seen the evidence behind some very popular
deceptions, but along the way you’ll also have picked up everything useful

第三層：
“you’ll also have picked up everything useful there is to know about research,
levels of evidence, bias, statistics, the history of science and anti-science
movements”

“But by the end of this book you’ll have the tools to win – or at least
understand – any argument you choose to initiate, whether it’s on miracle
cures, the evils of big pharma, the likelihood of a given vegetable preventing
cancer, and more. You’ll have seen the evidence behind some very popular
deceptions, but along the way you’ll also have picked up everything useful
there is to know about research, levels of evidence, bias, statistics, the
history of science and anti-science movements…”
這段可以分成三層：
第一層：
“you’ll have the tools to win – or at least understand – any argument”
Goldacre 說讀者會得到一些「工具」，用來贏得或至少理解爭論。
第二層：
“whether it’s on miracle cures, the evils of big pharma, the likelihood of a
given vegetable preventing cancer…”
這裡列出的是「你可能會爭論的題目」。
第三層：
“you’ll also have picked up everything useful there is to know about research,
levels of evidence, bias, statistics, the history of science and anti-science
movements”
這裡列出的是「你會學到的知識與分析工具」。
所以 Q57 的答案要從第三層找。

1. research
research 是工具，因為它讓讀者懂得研究如何產生證據。
Goldacre 的整本書都在教讀者不要只看 claim，要看 claim 背後的 research。
某個廣告、新聞標題、健康產品、另類療法可能說得很有科學感，但真正問題
是：
有沒有研究支持？
研究設計是否合理？
有沒有對照組？
結果是否重複出現？
研究是否由有利益關係的人資助？
樣本是否足夠？
所以 research 可以作為工具答案。
但如果你只寫：
science
這就比較弱。因為 science 太闊，原文工具清單中更具體的是 research。

2. levels of evidence
levels of evidence 指不同證據強弱的層級。
例如，在醫學和科學討論中：
個人經驗通常證據力較弱。
單一案例通常證據力有限。
小型研究比不上大型研究。
觀察性研究不一定能證明因果。
隨機對照試驗通常更有力。
系統性綜述或 meta-analysis 通常能提供更高層次的證據。
Goldacre 特別重視這一點，因為很多 bad science 的問題就在於人們把低層次
證據當成強證據。
例如：
一個人吃了某 supplement 後覺得精神好，這只是 anecdote。
某產品聲稱「很多人都說有效」，這不是強研究證據。
媒體把一個初步研究寫成重大突破，也可能誇大了 evidence level。
所以 levels of evidence 是非常貼合 “tools” 的答案。它比 “evidence” 單獨一字更
精準，因為原文寫的是 levels of evidence，重點在於判斷證據強弱，不只是看
見 evidence 這個概念。

3. bias
在 Goldacre 的語境中，bias 不是單純「偏見」這麼簡單。
它可以指研究、報道、判斷、選擇資料時出現的系統性偏差。
例如：
媒體只報道驚人的研究，不報道普通結果。
公司只公開對產品有利的研究。
研究設計本身可能讓結果偏向某一方。
讀者可能只相信自己本來想相信的東西。
治療有效的案例被放大，無效的案例被忽略。
懂得 bias，就能幫助讀者看穿很多 misleading claims。

What is Goldacre referring to when he says ‘along the way’?

Goldacre 所說的 “way” 是哪一個過程？

“way” 是一個 metaphorical learning journey

intellectual journey / reading journey / learning journey

在閱讀本書的過程中

題目問：
What does Goldacre mean when he says...
這是 implied meaning question。
它不是問字面意思，也不是問 style / flair 的字典解釋。
它要求你解釋這句話背後的真正含意，尤其要讀出作者語氣。
句子本身是：
you’ll still be wrong, but you’ll be wrong with a lot more style and flair than
you could possibly manage right now.
這句有幾個明顯特徵：
1. 它不是中性學術語氣。
2. 它帶幽默。
3. 它帶挑釁。
4. 它呼應前文 “you’ll have the tools”。
5. 它把 “wrong” 和 “style and flair” 放在一起，形成反差。
所以答案要處理兩層：
literal layer：Goldacre 說你仍然錯。
implied layer：但你會因讀過這本書而更懂辯論、更有知識地表達錯誤立場

常見錯誤
錯誤一：media = B。
媒體確實製造 noise，但 B 指被 noise 壓過的一方，應是 scientists and doctors。
錯誤二：alternative therapists = A。
他們也有誤導成分，但 A 的 money clue 明顯對應 £30 billion food supplements
industry。
錯誤三：British universities = D。
D 的 “nugget of truth” 對應 paragraph 11 的 “grain of science”，不是 universities。
Edmund Reading 技巧
Matching 題要抓 phrase-level paraphrase：
grain of science → nugget of truth
outnumbered and outgunned → struggle to be heard
routinely taught → being drilled
incapable of bearing reliable witness → incapable of communicating true picture
wrongness alongside genuine research → wrong and right together
不要只看同一個 topic word，要看 relation 是否一致。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Question
Is Goldacre optimistic or pessimistic about the future regarding science and
medicine? Use evidence from Text 5 to support your answer.
【Goldacre 對科學與醫學的未來是樂觀還是悲觀？請用 Text 5 的證據支持你的
答案。】
Goldacre is optimistic.
【Goldacre 是樂觀的。】
1. He believes readers can learn to challenge bad science.
2. Although he describes the present situation as very bad, the end of the
passage shows his belief that people can gain the tools to understand
evidence, statistics, bias and research.
3. He says that by the end of the book readers will have “the tools to win –
or at least understand – any argument”,
4. and that they will learn about “research, levels of evidence, bias, statistics”
and other useful ideas.
5. He also says that “the people making the stupid mistakes won’t be you”,
6. which shows his confidence that ordinary readers can improve their
understanding of science and medicine.
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Evidence 3: 他列出具體可學的工具
Paragraph 14 繼續說，讀者會學到：
“research, levels of evidence, bias, statistics, the history of science and
anti-science movements”
這一句比單純說 “you’ll be smarter” 更有力，
Goldacre 不是空泛鼓勵。他列出具體學習內容。
這些內容全部和科學與醫學理解有關：
Research 讀者會懂得研究如何產生證據。
levels of evidence
讀者會懂得不同證據強弱，不會把個人故事當成高質研究。
Bias 讀者會懂得研究、媒體、產業、個人判斷如何被偏差影響。
Statistics 讀者會懂得數據如何被誤解、誇大或操縱。
history of science 讀者會懂得科學怎樣發展、怎樣糾錯。
anti-science movements 讀者會懂得反科學思想如何運作。
這些全部是改善未來科學與醫學理解的工具。
Goldacre 相信普通讀者可以掌握它們，所以他的未來態度是 optimistic。

這些語言非常負面。

題目問的是 future。

arguments

“pessimistic”
如果學生答 pessimistic，通常會用以下 evidence：
● “how bad things have become”
● “outnumbered and outgunned”
● “hole in our culture is gaping”
● “grave consequences”
● “dangerous and grotesque extremes”
這些 evidence 的確真實，但它們回答的是：
Goldacre 如何看現況？
題目問：
Goldacre 如何看未來？
如果只用這些負面例子，答案會出現三個問題。
問題一：忽略題目中的 “future”
“how bad things have become” 是現在完成式，表示情況已發展到很差。
它不是未來判斷。
“outnumbered and outgunned” 也描述現在科學家與醫生被壓過。
這仍然是現況。
題目問 future，所以必須看文章結尾的 “you’ll...” statements。

常見錯誤三：把
“you’ll still be wrong”
當成
pessimism
Paragraph 15 最後說：
“you’ll still be wrong, but you’ll be wrong with a lot more style and flair”
這句也容易被誤讀。
有人會說：
他說讀者仍然 wrong，所以他很 pessimistic。
但完整看，這句帶幽默。
它的真正意思是：
即使你仍不同意，讀完後也會更有知識、更有技巧、更懂得辯論。
這句仍然包含 improvement：
● more style
● more flair
● better informed argument
● more sophisticated wrongness
所以它不是純悲觀。
它仍然承接前文的 reader improvement。

常見錯誤四：
把 寫成
optimism “science and medicine will
automatically improve”
這也不準。
Goldacre 的樂觀不是天真地說：
科學與醫學未來一定自然變好。
媒體一定會改善。
產業一定會變誠實。
公眾一定會突然明白 statistics。
他的樂觀集中在讀者與教育：
讀者如果讀這本書，就會得到 tools。
讀者可以 become critical。
讀者可以理解 evidence。
讀者可以識破 deception。
所以高分答案要寫：
He is optimistic because people can learn the tools to think critically.
不要寫：
He is optimistic because science and medicine will definitely improve by
themselves.
後者超出原文。
